title: Structured outputs (JSON, schemas)
notes: When code reads the answer, ask for JSON, not prose: a JSON schema fixes the fields, their types and the allowed values.
Pass the schema in output_config, or use Pydantic with messages.parse, and the reply comes back in that shape.
A valid shape is not a true answer: check the stop reason and the values, and route anything odd to a person.

slides.title: Structured outputs (JSON, schemas)
slides.sub: Why agents need data, not prose, and how a schema makes the model answer in a shape your code can trust
sentences: Scout can now answer customers clearly and within policy.
But an agent does more than talk: its code has to act on what the model says.
In this lesson you will get answers back as clean data, in a shape you define, that your code can trust.

slides.title: Prose versus data

left.label: Prose reply
points: Code has to guess what it means
One odd phrase breaks the program

right.label: JSON reply
points: Easy to check, store and route

sentences: So far, Scout has replied in sentences, which is perfect for customers and awkward for code.
Imagine your program must send each email to the right queue.
If the model says it sounds like a return, maybe urgent, your code has to guess what that means, and the wording changes every run.
One unexpected phrase, and the program breaks.
Now imagine the model answers in JSON, a simple text format of named fields and values.
Your code reads the intent field directly, the same way, every time.
Whenever code will act on the answer, ask for data, not prose.

slides.title: What is a JSON schema?
slides.definition: A description of the exact shape an answer must have: its fields, their types, and which ones are required.

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: A paper form with labelled boxes and tick-boxes: the model can only fill in what the form has room for.

sentences: To get reliable JSON, you describe the shape you want with a JSON schema.
A schema lists the fields, and the type of each one: text, a number, or true or false.
It can limit a field to a fixed list of allowed values, called an enum, such as return or exchange.
It says which fields are required, so none can go missing.
And it can forbid extra fields the model might like to add.
Think of a paper form with labelled boxes and tick-boxes: the model can only fill in what the form has room for.

slides.title: Scout's ticket schema
slides.lead: Four fields describe any customer email: intent, order_id, urgent and a one-line summary.

rows.out: an order number, or null if none
nothing extra; all four are required

aside.label: Null beats a guess
aside.text: Allowing null gives the model an honest way to say “no order number given” instead of inventing one.

sentences: Here is the schema you will build for Scout's ticket classifier.
Intent is text, but only one of five labels: where is order, return, exchange, product question or other.
Order ID is either text or null, which is JSON's word for nothing.
Urgent is a simple true or false, and summary is one line of text.
All four fields are required, and additional properties is set to false, so nothing extra sneaks in.
Allowing null matters: it gives the model an honest way to say there was no order number, instead of inventing one.

slides.title: Ask for it in the request
slides.lead: Add output_config with your schema. Then take the text block as usual and load it as JSON.

rows.out: the shape the reply must match

aside.label: Shape guaranteed
aside.text: The reply is constrained to the schema: no chatter around the JSON, no missing fields.

sentences: Now you pass that schema with the request.
Add an output config whose format is a JSON schema, and hand it your ticket schema.
The model's answer is then constrained to match that shape, field for field.
You take the text block as usual, and load it with Python's json module.
Now you have an ordinary Python dictionary, and its intent field might say return, with no order number beside it.
There is no chatter around the JSON and no missing field, so your code can read it directly.

slides.title: Three ways to ask for structure
sentences: There are three ways to ask for structure, from weakest to strongest.
You can simply ask for JSON in the prompt, which usually works, but sometimes arrives wrapped in a friendly sentence.
You can pass a JSON schema in the output config, which guarantees the shape, and load the text yourself.
Or you can describe the ticket as a Python class with Pydantic, a popular library for checking data.
Then you call messages parse with that class as the output format, and the parsed output arrives as a ready-made object.
The last two do the same job, so pick whichever style your project already uses.

slides.title: Validate anyway

nodes.label: Act or flag
nodes.sub: route it, or ask a person

note.text: A valid shape is not a true answer. The model gives structure; your code owns the decisions.

sentences: One last habit: validate anyway.
The schema guarantees the shape of the answer, not that the answer is true.
So check what matters, such as whether the order number looks like a real Orbit order number.
Check the stop reason too, because a reply cut off at max tokens may not be complete JSON.
If a check fails, do not guess: send the ticket to a person, or ask the model again.
The model gives you structure, and your code still owns the decisions.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: When code reads the answer, ask for JSON, not prose
A schema fixes the fields, their types, allowed values and required fields
Pass it in output_config, or use Pydantic with messages.parse
A valid shape is not a true answer: check, then act or hand over

sentences: Let us pull it together.
Whenever code will act on the answer, ask for JSON instead of prose.
A JSON schema fixes the fields, their types, the allowed values and which ones are required.
Pass it in the output config, or use a Pydantic class with messages parse.
And validate anyway, because a valid shape is not the same as a true answer.
In the guided practice, you will build exactly this: a classifier that turns Orbit's emails into clean JSON.

midQuiz.q: Why do agents need JSON rather than a friendly sentence?
options: Code acts on the answer, and JSON has fixed fields it can read the same way every time
midQuiz.explain: Prose changes wording every run; JSON fields stay put, so code can read and act on them reliably.
midQuiz.hint: In an agent, who reads the answer first: a customer, or your program?

midQuiz.q: In Scout's schema, why can order_id be null?
options: So the model can say no order number was given, instead of inventing one
Because null takes fewer tokens than a string
Because Orbit's orders don't have numbers
midQuiz.explain: Without null, the field must hold a string, so the model has to put something there even when nothing was given.
midQuiz.hint: Think back to the hook: what does a model do with a gap and no honest way to say so?

endQuiz.q: The JSON matches the schema perfectly, but order_id is ORB-99999, which doesn't exist. What does this show?
options: A valid shape is not a true answer, so code still checks the facts
Structured outputs should be turned off
endQuiz.explain: The schema guarantees the shape, not the truth. Your code checks values before acting, and routes anything odd to a person.
endQuiz.hint: What exactly does a schema promise?

endQuiz.q: Which change turns "please reply in JSON" into a guarantee?
options: Adding ONLY JSON in capitals to the prompt
Passing a JSON schema in output_config
endQuiz.explain: A schema in output_config constrains the reply to that shape. A request in the prompt usually works, but not always.
endQuiz.hint: One option changes the request itself, not just the wording of the prompt.
